Thanks for submitting, my github isn't necessarily about getting the most FPS and overclocking. It's about stability, research, and guidelines with a lot of reputable technical references to help you decide what's best for you.

If you can, make your way into Latency & Gaming discord. 
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7385812/131223910-0f08751e-8941-45f8-a874-7aab2926c167.png)

In that case, I would like you to make that explicit on the page. In the first line, people see the "optimizing your gaming PC, configuration and setup" and think of increasing their PC's performance and not necessarily making their PC last for a long time. Maybe "optimizing for stability" or "maximizing stability" could work as a way to show that?

This takes me back to the 'disabling Turbo Boost' step. I can now understand that it's for stability purposes, but for people reading the guide it will be a turn-off.

Also. why do you want me to join the L&G discord?

Hopefully people aren't just reading the first line then skipping the bullet point summary and objectives. :D 

Optimizing really implies many things such as reducing and controlling variables which perhaps could improve performance, stability/reliability. The guide itself is just that, a guideline and ideally a good starting point for people.

For Turbo Boost what do you think about something like this?

**Turbo Boost**
- If isolating performance behavior issues, disable.
- If you'd like to use Turbo Boost frequencies I'd recommend using a static overclock to reduce minor overhead from dynamic frequency scaling, otherwise enable.

Looks good enough for me. I would want to have the first line to be a bit more descriptive in order for readers to know what exact definition of 'optimizing' we're using instead of just hoping they read more in-depth, but that's just my opinion; since no one else complained about it, you can leave that first sentence be.

Also. why do you want me to join the L&G discord?
A good discord on all things performance and latency.

I edited my previous response to be less grumpy.

For context, what motivated me to read and contribute to this guide is exactly the evidence based nature of it.

Plausibly beneficial changes are functionally superstition, and superstition can snowball into pure pseudoscience. See the audiophile community, and most "increase fps" discussions found on reddit and youtube.

Sticking to what can be demonstrated is a worthy goal.

Thanks for the feedback so far and AMIT for commenting.

Disabling RGB 
- RGB and related power sources have been known to cause audio interference but it "depends". Then there's situations like Corsair iCUE which previously required their software to be running all the time to control it, less software running the better. I'd be ok with stating something along those lines that "you may enable RGB after all optimizations and testing have been complete, then test again for impacts to your benchmarks and experience". Generally the fewer the variables the better.

Flow Control
- Works similarly to TCP Window Size by notifying a transmitter to reduce or to delay sending data being sent, it requests a system to buffer data temporarily until congestion is reduced or the receiver can allow it. There's other things at play here as well to handle congestion built into operating systems and routers.
- Intel recommends disabling Flow Control here but indicates you could drop packets as a result, likely under extreme load.
  - https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/support/articles/000005811/ethernet-products.html
- https://blog.cloudflare.com/how-to-achieve-low-latency/ 
  - "flow control [...] it can introduce unpredictable latency spikes during higher load"
- Many games rely on UDP which is a connectionless protocol, send and hope it gets there. No guarantees anyways.
- When playing competitively ideal conditions would be playing on an unsaturated local network over the internet. Turn off other network devices for best case for localized variables. QoS or packet priority scheduling algorithms can help with higher throughput networks if you have no control of network usage. fq_codel, cake etc. Bufferbloat problem.
- For Flow Control to work, connected routers, and devices must also support it and have it enabled.

NVIDIA Recommendations
- I'll review more closely but could be reasonable to update it as suggested. No ETA right now.

SpeedShift and SpeedStep (EIST)
- These are power saving and efficiency features to manage voltage and frequency based on workload, one implemented in hardware the other software.
- Typically the concern here is transition times between those states could impact performance in comparison to a static voltage and frequency configuration.
- "Some of the sources linked explicitly advise against this" feel free to provide reference and refresh my memory.

GameMode
- It has some benefits but often those benefits are taken care of by careful optimizations, disabling windows updates and background processes which may also cause notifications. 
- You can use Windows Performance Recorder and Analyzer to see when GameMode is engaged, I haven't done much testing around it personally but it seems more useful for casual gamers than competitive with optimized systems. Feel free to add more context if you have some references.

Steam Path Anti-Virus Exclusion
- Thanks, yes pros and cons to this one, I can revisit.

I updated [this page](https://github.com/BoringBoredom/PC-Optimization-Hub/blob/main/content/xhci%20imod/xhci%20imod.md) with a guide since the one in this repository is partially incorrect. `Runtime Register Space Offset` is 32 bits instead of 16 bits and located at +0x18 instead of +18 (the red number in RWE is a decimal, not hex). It was just a coincidence that both values were 0x2000 in that specific case.

(32 * 0) is Interrupter 0, (32 * 1) is Interrupter 1, etc. In that example, the mouse was on Interrupter 4 (32 * 4). You either have to set all IMOD registers to 0 or figure out a way to automatically determine which one is responsible for the mouse.
![image](https://github.com/djdallmann/GamingPCSetup/assets/16615327/5efd5234-2284-46cb-aab5-e24057fdffea)

Everything you need to know is explained in the screenshots of the xHCI documentation. Take your time to read and understand it, otherwise you won't understand what I was talking about in my earlier posts.

I had a brief look at your script and it seems overly complicated, you should be able to disable IMOD with a lot less lines than what you have. I would like to try out of interest, what method are you using to read the value at a given address in general?

Regarding my question, I was wondering as to how you are reading addresses. You can read addresses from CLI with:

```bat
.\RW.exe /Command="R32 <address>" /Stdout
```

For determining the amount of interrupters, I think you can count the amount of IRQs the device is using but i'm not totally sure so don't quote me on that. Everything is the same for AMD, I tested it on another system.

https://www.amd.com/system/files/TechDocs/51192_Bolton_FCH_RRG.pdf

Apologies, I didn't see that you included the snippet in your script. 

Without determining the amount of interrupters, it is difficult to determine how many addresses to iterate over to disable IMOD for.

> Not if it's changing when mouse are moving (that is not possible to see data wise). Only visually and in realtime.

You could check whether the IMOD counter is > 0.
I built a script to disable imod usb.

The docs mention that there can be *up to* 1024 interrupters, meaning there may not be 1024. I haven't looked into this that much but I don't think assuming there are always a fixed amount of interrupters is a good idea because you may be spilling into another address space in case the space is dynamic. If it is fixed then I guess it is fine but as I said, haven't looked into it that much.

> The Interrupter logic consists of an Interrupter Management Register, an Interrupter Moderation Register, and the Event Ring Registers. A one to one mapping is defined for Interrupter to MSI-X vector. Up to 1024 Interrupters are supported.

On the other hand, the AMD docs mention that there can be *up to* 8 interrupters. You can't really continue without determining the amount of interrupters to disable IMOD for.

> First interrupter has 7 32-bit positions, while every other after, have 8

They're all 8x4 bytes.

> the address could be anywhere in any position from / in any interrupter

The IMOD register is always in the same spot within an interrupter: `Runtime Base + 0x24 + (32 * interrupter index)`

![image](https://github.com/djdallmann/GamingPCSetup/assets/16615327/65ad6a30-e56c-440e-91be-f2a27454b2b0)
![image](https://github.com/djdallmann/GamingPCSetup/assets/16615327/95a0fbf2-bf5f-4045-aa5d-e8218af57e98)

As mentioned before, you can't assume that there will be a fixed amount of interrupters. For example, there is nothing at interrupter 1023 on my system. I wouldn't be comfortable with a script modifying random addresses.

![image](https://github.com/djdallmann/GamingPCSetup/assets/86924251/bd158829-ebbe-4322-8183-1b635963b753)

What has this got to do with IMOD? https://github.com/dougg0k/gaming_os_tweaker/blob/2c6ed3295e2ed539d9c5b5aa7fdf9b0fa3186b3c/scripts/optional_helpers/interrupt_moderation_usb.ps1#L108-L114

On another note, nobody has been able to demonstrate whether that *actually* does anything.

That doesn't contain information for those registry entries. They have been polluting the internet for a while and a lot of people seem to use them without real evidence that it has any effect so I was wondering whether someone finally had any. On the other hand, Windows Internals specifies that ``DevicePriority`` changes IRQ priorities which can I believe can be verified in WinDbg.

![image](https://github.com/djdallmann/GamingPCSetup/assets/86924251/d011b949-a8e1-4804-9672-2edd24df1c86)

> both are able to affect devices

Do you have any evidence or official documentation for the registry entries affecting anything? At least ``DevicePriority`` is officially documented. As far as i'm concerned, those ``IRQXPriority`` entries are made up until anyone is able to prove otherwise.

> Where one is for IRQ (not only devices) and the DevicePriority are for devices only.

Windows Internals mention that it controls IRQ priorities per-device though.

> I guess it somewhat make sense to be in this script too

I completely disagree. I wouldn't expect a script that was intended to disable xHCI interrupt moderation to mess with IRQ priorities. The topics are completely unrelated.

> if the changes only are microseconds, most would probably not be able to truly do

I'm not talking about benchmarks, I mean whether the setting has any feedback within the OS (e.g. WinDbg). Benchmarking introduces variables which may lead to invalid conclusions in the scenario where there are differences in scores with A vs. B while the registry entry does not even exist.

Some *tweaks* have negative effects too. Without understanding or justifying the change, it wouldn't be appropriate to apply it to a system in my opinion. Especially if it is being generalised in a script for all systems while every system is different. It is not that big of a deal with a non-existent registry key but helps to prevent spreading false information around the internet. With this mindset, nobody will keep track of what is making a system perform worse or better.

The Intel docs demonstrate how the amount of interrupters can be determined. You can also refer to BoringBoredom's updated page. The bits 18:8 align with  ``!usb3kd.xhci_capability`` in WinDbg.

![image](https://github.com/djdallmann/GamingPCSetup/assets/86924251/45852487-e70a-46c2-9012-a304abec5846)
Well, the info was in the Intel docs to begin with. It also seems consistent with other vendors.

> I haven't done much testing around [Game Mode] personally but it seems more useful for casual gamers than competitive with optimized systems

I have indeed been approaching this as more of an end user, I definitely agree that a specific purpose use machine doesn't need to keep EIST and SST enabled. I also don't have further specifics of what game mode does at this time, and agree that it represents potential behavioral uncertainty, particularly as updates change its behavior in the future.

For some reason at the time I wrote the commit I generalized "streaming video".

The specific impact that I observed was to game streaming, which I make use of over LAN. I recognize that the guide recommends disabling this in Steam.

I use Sunshine Game Stream (the foss replacement server to nvidia gamestream) and Moonlight as my client. With flow control disabled on the host, packet loss was so high no stream could be transmitted, unless I restricted the bitrate such that bandwidth did not exceed 5mbps.

I suspect this would also impact streaming from OBS to twitch or youtube or other.

> Pretty much the only thing left is to verify in different OSs. If it's grabbing the interrupters addresses correctly. To know if the implementation are correct / accurate.

The address will always be correct assuming you have the correct offsets and that they are consistent across vendors.

> I am on Win11 22h2 with the new high pooling rate fixes. Not sure if the changes reached imod though.

The updated input stack is unrelated to xHCI interrupt moderation. [It limits the raw input listening rate for background processes](https://twitter.com/amitxv/status/1666157717759877120).

> I use Sunshine Game Stream (the foss replacement server to nvidia gamestream) and Moonlight as my client. With flow control disabled on the host, packet loss was so high no stream could be transmitted, unless I restricted the bitrate such that bandwidth did not exceed 5mbps.

Thanks for adding context! Btw can you tell me more about your network, ISP up/down speed, any QoS (in Windows/Router etc?), are all systems involved 1000Gbps? Any on Wifi? Do you have double NAT, Internet <-> ISP (NAT) <-> Personal Router (NAT) <-> Desktops?

I (near) exclusively stream in-LAN, using it primarily as an RDP alternative.

My typical bandwidth needs are 20mbps, and the host PC is wired but the clients are often wireless.

I observed the issue from two laptops and my phone, and I do not have QoS enabled on any computer or the router, which is an Edgerouter X paired with U6-IW.

Keeping in mind the problem was a direct connection over (W)LAN, and Flow Control off unambiguously led to a severe and un-ignorible plummet in performance:
